Rampart
ram'part
n. (the outer defensive mound or bulwark of a fortified city; in Lamentations made to mourn, and in Nahum shown to be no defence at all)
French rempart, from remparer, to fortify. The Hebrew chel denotes the outer rampart or fore-wall, the earthwork standing before the wall proper — the first line, not the last.

Biblical Definition

Lamentations personifies the defences of a doomed city: “The LORD hath purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion: he hath stretched out a line, he hath not withdrawn his hand from destroying: therefore he made the rampart and the wall to lament; they languished together” (Lamentations 2:8). Two things stand out. The destroyer is named — the LORD purposed it, and stretched out the measuring line, which is the builder's instrument turned to demolition. And the fortifications themselves mourn. Nahum makes the argument explicit against Nineveh by pointing at an earlier casualty: “Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea?” (Nahum 3:8). Thebes had the best rampart imaginable — the Nile itself — and Ethiopia and Egypt for allies, “and it was infinite” (Nahum 3:9), and Thebes fell. The argument runs from the greater to the lesser: if that city could not stand, Nineveh cannot. No earthwork is a defence when the LORD has stretched out the line.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a rampart as an elevation of earth round a place, serving to cover it from the fire of an enemy, and a bulwark as a rampart or fortification.

expand to see more

RAMPART, n. In fortification, an elevation or mound of earth round a place, capable of resisting the cannon of an enemy.

2. That which fortifies and defends from assault; that which secures safety.

BULWARK, n. In fortification, a bastion, or a rampart; a mound of earth round a place, capable of resisting cannon shot.

FORTIFY, v.t. To surround with a wall, ditch, palisades or other works, with a view to defend against the attacks of an enemy.

LANGUISH, v.i. To lose strength or animation; to be or to become dull, feeble or spiritless.

Key Scripture

Lamentations 2:8 — "The LORD hath purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion: he hath stretched out a line, he hath not withdrawn his hand from destroying: therefore he made the rampart and the wall to lament; they languished together."

Nahum 3:8 — "Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea?"

Nahum 3:9 — "Ethiopia and Egypt were her strength, and it was infinite; Put and Lubim were thy helpers."

Lamentations 2:9 — "Her gates are sunk into the ground; he hath destroyed and broken her bars: her king and her princes are among the Gentiles: the law is no more; her prophets also find no vision from the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Security is sought in the defences themselves, and Lamentations names the LORD as the one who purposed their fall.

expand to see more

Lamentations 2:8 is a hard verse for any theology that will not say God does the destroying. The prophet does not describe Babylon breaching a wall; he says the LORD hath purposed to destroy, and stretched out the line, and did not withdraw His hand. Modern treatments regularly soften this into permission — God allowed it, God did not prevent it — which is not what the text says and not what the Confession says either: God ordains whatsoever comes to pass, and is neither the author of sin nor a bystander to history. The men who broke that wall were wicked and were fully responsible; the purpose was the LORD's. Lamentations is written by someone who believed both and wept anyway.

The practical corruption is the one Nahum attacks: trusting the rampart. Thebes had the Nile for a moat and infinite allies, and fell. Nineveh had walls that were the wonder of the age, and fell within a generation of the prophecy. Every institution builds ramparts — endowments, reputations, legal protections, structures designed so that nothing can go badly wrong — and Scripture's consistent judgment is that these are exactly as strong as God permits and no stronger. Lamentations 2:9 shows what the fall of a rampart actually costs: the law is no more, and her prophets find no vision. That is the loss to grieve, and no earthwork ever protected it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chel, an outer rampart or fore-wall — Lamentations 2:8, Nahum 3:8, Psalm 122:7; chomah, the wall proper; No, the city of Thebes in Egypt.

expand to see more

Hebrew chel — a rampart, the outer fortification; Lamentations 2:8, Nahum 3:8, and Psalm 122:7 where peace is prayed within it.

Hebrew chomah — a city wall; paired with the rampart in Lamentations 2:8, and they languish together.

Hebrew qav — a measuring line; Lamentations 2:8, the builder's tool used for demolition.

Hebrew No — Thebes, the Egyptian capital on the Nile; Nahum 3:8, and Jeremiah 46:25.

Nahum 3:10 completes the argument: yet was she carried away, she went into captivity.

Usage

"“He made the rampart and the wall to lament; they languished together”."

"“Whose rampart was the sea” — the best defence imaginable, and it fell."

"“The LORD hath purposed to destroy” — not permitted; purposed."
